articles.title: No further action against government adviser's wife over Palestine Action post, police say
articles.summary: Sarah Helm, who is married to Jonathan Powell, was responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney.
articles.body:
Police say no further action will be taken against the wife of the government's national security adviser after she posted on social media referencing Palestine Action.

Sarah Helm, who is married to Jonathan Powell, wrote on X on Thursday: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

She was responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support the proscribed organisation.

On Saturday, the Metropolitan Police said Helm's post was "assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold".

"No further police action will be taken," the force added.

On Friday, the Met Police had said it was "in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required" after it was "made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action".

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025. Support of the group is a criminal offence and punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Best-selling author Rooney said she would donate earnings from her books to the group, which has a stated goal of "ending global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".

As a result, Rooney's publisher, Faber, determined it could not sell her novels, including Normal People and Conversations with Friends, in the UK.

articles.title: 19 killed in Kolkata stampede; CM Suvendu announces jobs, Rs 25 lakh for kin
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday announced a compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a government job for the family of each
articles.body: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday announced a compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a government job for the family of each person killed in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata.The state government will also bear the entire cost of medical treatment for the injured and provide Rs 5 lakh to each of them, Adhikari said, adding that a fact-finding committee would be constituted to investigate the incident."This is a tragic incident. 19 people have lost their lives, 17 of whom died on the spot... 25 people have been injured; 24 of them are out of danger, while one remains in critical condition," the chief minister said. He added that the government was making every possible effort to assist the affected families and that he had personally met relatives of the deceased.'Appropriate measures against those who failed to manage crowd'Adhikari said the state government would seek the intervention of the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to constitute a fact-finding committee, which would include special task force (STF) and forensic teams. The investigation would examine the circumstances leading to the stampede and identify those responsible for the crowd management arrangements.Kolkata Police's Anti-Rowdy Section (ARS) has collected CCTV footage from the site, which will be examined as part of the investigation."We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.He said the state government was making arrangements for postmortems in accordance with the law and that six of the deceased had been identified so far. Officials were also coordinating with the families of the victims.The chief minister said the families who had met him had expressed faith in the state government. He added that the Prime Minister's Office had sought a report from the chief secretary, which had been submitted, and that the Centre and the state were working together to provide assistance.'Some attempting to politicise this, but it will be to no avail'Adhikari also criticised the previous state government over its handling of past tragedies, accusing some people of attempting to politicise the current incident."Everyone is well aware of the role of the previous government in similar incidents that occurred in the past. Some are attempting to politicize this, but it will be to no avail. I have met with the families of the deceased, and they have explicitly stated that they have full faith in the Chief Minister and the government... The PMO also requested a report from the Chief Secretary, which we have submitted. The Prime Minister has announced relief and compensation. The central and state governments are working together on this..." he said.Referring to other incidents, Adhikari said 13 people had died due to electrocution during the 2025 Puja season amid heavy rain. He also referred to a devastating flood in north Bengal that killed 100 people, questioning the previous chief minister's response to those tragedies.'An announcement by the organisers' led to the rushThe stampede occurred on Saturday evening, on Maha Saptami, at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata. At least 19 people died and 25 were injured after a crowd surge amid rain, according to officials.A police officer said people waiting outside the pandal rushed forward as it began raining, causing some to fall on the road and triggering the stampede. Adhikari said an announcement made by the organisers of the community Durga Puja had led to a rush among revellers, resulting in what he described as a "painful incident".Officials of the organising club, private security guards and personnel on duty were detained for questioning, he said. The administration also advised several crowded theme-based puja pandals to temporarily close following the tragedy.Union home minister Amit Shah, who had arrived in Kolkata and was scheduled to visit pandals on Sunday, cancelled his programmes following the incident. President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Shah and former chief minister Mamata Banerjee expressed condolences over the deaths.PM Modi announced an ex gratia payment of Rs 2 lakh for the next of kin of each deceased person and Rs 50,000 for each injured person. The state government has also launched a toll-free helpline to provide information related to the stampede.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
articles.summary: There were violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police throughout Saturday in the capital Tirana.
articles.body:
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.

Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.

The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.

Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement , with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.

Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.

The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.

During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.

Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.

Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.

Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.

Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.

As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.

Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.

The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.

George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.

He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.

In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.

Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.

"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution.

"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."

Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.

She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."

She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.

Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.

The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?

Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".

The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.

In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".

He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.

He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.

The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.

Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.

Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.

She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.

Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.

Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.

Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.

"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.

"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."

Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

articles.body: It had the makings of another classic home win at Darrell K. Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium. The Longhorns were up 17-3 after Ryan Niblett returned a punt for a touchdown to give the Horns a two-score lead midway through the second quarter while their opponent, the Florida Gators, looked hapless. Then something flipped. TEXAS LONGHORNS FAVORED BY 11.5 OVER FLORIDA GATORS DESPITE BACK-TO-BACK STRUGGLES IN SEC FOOTBALL The Gators buckled down, adopting the hard-nosed mentality that head coach Jon Sumrall has been trying to impart on them since their blowout loss to Missouri two weeks ago, and outscored Texas 24-7 over the final two and a half quarters to nab a signature win. Florida could have easily folded, especially given the two-game losing streak they came in on, coupled with the loss of starting quarterback Aaron Philo and top wideout Vernell Brown III. Instead, the Gators turned to Tramell Jones, making his first collegiate start in a venue that has not been kind to opposing teams or quarterbacks. Jones turned in a yeoman's effort, going 22-35 for 155 passing yards and two touchdowns while also keeping the Longhorn defense honest with his legs. Running back Jadan Baugh started to look like his old self as well (25 carries for 91 yards and a score), which certainly helped Florida and Jones by extension. Starting with their quarterback, Arch Manning once again looked less than adequate for large stretches of the game. Outside of a massive 62-yard pass on 4th and 7 late in the game, Manning had just over 100 yards through the air. Give some credit to Florida's defensive line for harassing the junior signal caller for much of the day, but the Gators' pass defense has ranked in the 100s in most statistical categories and was supposed to represent a "get right" opportunity for Manning. Instead, the beleaguered quarterback continues to slide down mock draft boards as the season matures. Another loss would almost certainly mean the end of the Longhorns' College Football Playoff hopes, and missing the postseason tournament two years in a row would be unacceptable for a team as talented as Texas. Many pundits were ready to put Sarkisian on the hot seat to start the season, and if he doesn't turn things around in a hurry in Austin, he could very well be on his way out. All the pieces were in place for the Longhorns to make a run at the title this fall, but a loss today puts everything on life support. articles.title: Senedd member says smart glasses help with speeches in the Senedd
articles.summary: Jason O'Connell sparked debate when he started wearing the glasses, which have an autocue feature.
articles.body:
A Reform politician says he is using smart glasses with an in-built autocue feature to help him make speeches in the Welsh Parliament.

Jason O'Connell said the technology had helped boost his confidence when speaking in the Senedd, and denied it risked misleading people into thinking he was speaking without notes.

"I'm delivering my words in the manner that I see fit," he told the BBC's Politics Wales programme.

But the Welsh Liberal Democrat leader called for the glasses to be banned from use in the Senedd, while a parliament spokesperson said a review was under way.

They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image?

The Meta glasses revolution - is it okay to film people in public?

The smart glasses have allowed O'Connell to make speeches by reading a digital script that appears on the lenses of his glasses.

The text scrolls as he speaks, and it can also be controlled via a ring on his finger.

The Senedd member for the Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr constituency said he had been looking at ways to improve his oratory skills since being elected to the parliament in May.

He said: "One of the things I identified as a weakness of mine was that my head was down looking at my notes a lot, and I wanted to get away from that and these glasses enable me to do that."

Asked if he risked misleading people by giving the impression he was speaking without notes, O'Connell said: "I'm delivering my words in the manner that I see fit.

"Other people might use an iPad, they might use a phone, they might use printed paper.

"This is the method that I find works best for me during those long debates.

"This is authentically my voice, and it's just me relaying that in the way that I feel most comfortable."

O'Connell said the glasses had boosted his confidence "massively".

"As a new member we do have to get over that hurdle and the more of these you do the more confident you get," he said.

"It enables me to communicate effectively with the constituents, the people of Wales.

"When I'm scrutinising government, I want to be able to look the government in the face."

However, concerns have been raised about the use of the technology, particularly ones that have a camera and can record video - although O'Connell's glasses do not have a camera.

Welsh Lib Dem leader Jane Dodds said not enough was known yet about what the glasses could do, and said Members of the Senedd (MSs) needed to have equal access to their use.

"What I've called for is that there is a ban on the use of smart glasses in the Welsh Parliament until we have rules and regulations in place which standardise them, and make sure that everybody can have access to them, if that's what they want as well," she said.

A spokesperson for the Senedd's presiding officer said: "Rapidly advancing technologies such as smart glasses offer opportunities to improve accessibility and support Members of the Senedd in their work, but we recognise that they also prompt concerns.

"A review of the use of this technology on the Senedd estate is under way, and we will bring forward its conclusions shortly."

articles.title: Martha's Vineyard rejected a 54-acre subdivision with 26 below-market lots and 19 luxury homes after seven marathon meetings, leaving land bought for $6.6 million in 2017 undeveloped for now
articles.summary: Martha’s Vineyard has rejected one of the largest housing proposals ever considered by its regional planning body.
articles.body: Martha’s Vineyard has rejected one of the largest housing proposals ever considered by its regional planning body. The Katama Meadows project in Edgartown proposed 52 homes across 54 acres, including 26 below-market lots intended for moderate-income residents and municipal workers, alongside 19 market-rate homes that could have sold for around $5 million each. After seven lengthy meetings, the Martha’s Vineyard Commission voted 10 to 3, with one abstention, to deny the project.The decision leaves the land, purchased by Utah developers Richard Matthews and Douglas Anderson for $6.6 million in 2017, undeveloped for now. According to The Martha’s Vineyard Times (MVTimes), commissioners said the parcel will remain as it is unless the developers submit a new plan, though they indicated during the final session that another proposal is likely. Read more details about this, as per MVTimes here:A proposal meant to ease housing pressureKatama Meadows was designed as a mixed-income subdivision off Meshacket Way and Division Road in Edgartown. It included 52 homesite lots, with 26 described as attainable or affordable homes for moderate-income earners and municipal workers. Twelve lots were to be sold for $225,000 each, while 14 were to be donated to the town of Edgartown.The plan also set aside lots for Habitat for Humanity. Its supporters argued that it would create much-needed “missing middle” housing for people such as police officers, teachers, firefighters and emergency medical workers, who often earn too much to qualify for traditional affordable housing but cannot afford the island’s high market-rate prices.The developers had already revised the proposal several times. Their earlier plan, called Meetinghouse Place, proposed 24 market-rate homes and was denied by the commission in 2020. The fourth version added donated and income-restricted lots, a change that won support from the Edgartown Select Board, the town’s Affordable Housing Committee and the fire department.Environmental concerns became decisiveDespite that local support, the project faced strong opposition from residents, conservationists and several commissioners. The land borders Edgartown Great Pond, a watershed already impaired by nitrogen pollution. Commissioners were concerned that new homes and septic systems would add nitrogen to the pond, even if the development connected to town sewer lines and included mitigation measures.Nitrogen pollution can contribute to eutrophication, a process that reduces oxygen in ponds and can create conditions harmful to fish, wildlife and the broader ecosystem. The commission ultimately designated Katama Meadows a full detriment to the environment, citing both water-quality concerns and the loss of carbon sequestration from clearing woodland.Tisbury commissioner Ben Robinson said the location was wrong for development because the parcel functions as a wildlife corridor. Other commissioners argued that the island’s environmental limits must shape housing policy, even when the need for homes is urgent.Concerns over luxury homes and segregationThe market-rate portion of the proposal also drew criticism. Commissioners noted that the 19 market-rate lots, each larger than 4,000 square feet, could support homes priced around $5 million and marketed to seasonal or year-round buyers. Critics worried that such homes would add to the island’s stock of luxury properties without solving the housing shortage for year-round residents.Commissioners also objected to the separation of income-restricted and market-rate lots within the subdivision. West Tisbury commissioner Linda Sibley called the income-segregated design offensive, while Chilmark commissioner Joan Malkin questioned whether the island should pursue more “missing middle” housing at the expense of affordable homes.Supporters countered that the trade-off was necessary. Commissioner Doug Sederholm argued that securing homes for 26 island families and preserving about 32 acres of woodland was worth accepting 19 luxury homes for off-island buyers. He warned that rejecting the project could lead to a worse proposal in the future.Why the decision mattersThe vote came after what The Martha’s Vineyard Times described as the longest final deliberation in the commission’s history. Commissioners weighed environmental impact, housing need, traffic, health and safety, night lighting, the local economy, social development and recreation before reaching their final decision.The outcome reflects a broader dilemma facing resort and coastal communities: how to provide housing for the workers who keep local services running without allowing development that worsens environmental damage or increases seasonal luxury ownership. More than 60 percent of Martha’s Vineyard’s housing stock is used for two months or less each year, according to figures cited during the hearings.Aquinnah commissioner Jannette Vanderhoop argued that the island’s housing crisis is not simply a shortage of homes but a lack of access. That view shaped the commission’s conclusion that Katama Meadows, despite its affordable component, was not the right solution for the island at this location.What happens nextFor now, the 54-acre site remains undeveloped. The developers still own the land and may return with a revised application, but the commission’s rejection sets a significant precedent for how Martha’s Vineyard evaluates large housing projects.The decision also leaves unresolved the question of how the island will house its essential workers. Katama Meadows offered one possible answer, but commissioners concluded that its environmental cost, luxury-market component and design did not meet the island’s needs. The debate over where and how to build is likely to continue.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Internet is fundamental right of all, even children: Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Raising citizens’ right to access and use of internet to the level of fundamental right, Supreme Court has held that even children are entitled
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Raising citizens’ right to access and use of internet to the level of fundamental right, Supreme Court has held that even children are entitled to that right and said it does not endorse imposing in the name of safety a blanket ban on children accessing internet. At the same time, it favoured restricting access to content that is inherently harmful to kids.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Chandran said that right to access and use of the internet is part of Article 21 (right to life and liberty) and Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression). The internet is “priceless” as it provides access to information and education to all in even remote areas, where it is often the only source of learning for many children. Noting that the SC had earlier refrained from expressing a definitive view on whether the right to access the internet is, by itself, a fundamental right, the bench said, “...we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.”SC: Internet’s value priceless, efficacy of curbs not provedSC said, “Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or freedom of speech worth expressing.”The order was passed on a public interest litigationfiled by NGO ‘Just Rights for Children Alliance’, which highlights continued lapses by intermediaries in tackling child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) despite SC’s 2024 judgment in this regard.Agreeing with its plea, SC said there has been “no progress worth the name” in the last two years.Acknowledging that there has been “a growing yet short-lived tendency across the globe in the recent past to limit the access of children below a certain age to the internet, more particularly to social media platforms,” SC said, “we too gave this our anxious consideration, and only thereafter, we decided consciously not to endorse the same”.It said the efficacy of such restrictive measures remains far from established in countries which have imposed them.“... Children do not cease to use the internet merely because the law prohibits them from doing so ... They move to other platforms and websites that are unregulated and even more unsafe,” SC said.“All that we are trying to say is that any blanket restriction on access to internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality. No jurisdiction has, so far, been able to demonstrate that children are any safer on account of such measures,” it said.It said some age-based restrictions and safeguards should exist for the safety of children online.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Ross Perot Jr. began buying Texas land in 1985; his vision helped transform Fort Worth
articles.summary: In the 1980s, much of northern Fort Worth consisted of farms, ranches and open prairie. Ross Perot Jr.
articles.body: In the 1980s, much of northern Fort Worth consisted of farms, ranches and open prairie. Ross Perot Jr. saw an opportunity to transform the largely rural landscape into a major business and transport centre. He began buying the land that became AllianceTexas in 1985, laying the foundations for a development that would eventually cover 27,000 acres. Over the following decades, the project attracted hundreds of companies, an industrial airport, freight facilities, warehouses, corporate campuses and residential communities. Here’s how Perot's long-term vision helped change the region's economic landscape.Ross Perot Jr.'s early land purchases laid the foundations for AllianceTexasRoss Perot Jr. began buying the land that became Alliance in 1985, when much of the area north of Fort Worth remained rural. According to Hillwood's retrospective, published on 20 December 2024, the property eventually formed part of a 27,000-acre development along Interstate 35W. At the time, comparable land around Dallas was significantly more expensive. Perot told the Fort Worth Star-Telegram that many families who sold him their ranches were the first generation to do so, unlike landowners in the Dallas area, where properties had often changed hands repeatedly.The scale of the acquisition gave Perot room to pursue a long-term development plan. Rather than building a single commercial project, he envisioned a destination where aviation, industry, transport and businesses could operate alongside one another. The development's success was far from guaranteed. Perot invested in land before the area had attracted the number of companies that would eventually establish operations there. His decision laid the groundwork for one of North Texas's largest planned developments.How the industrial airport helped turn Perot's vision into realityA major milestone came on 14 December 1989, when Fort Worth Alliance Airport opened. Perot had agreed to provide land for an airport after the Federal Aviation Administration identified a need for additional aviation capacity in the Dallas-Fort Worth region. His aviation contacts advised that the area would benefit from an industrial airport rather than one focused on general aviation. The airport was intended to support freight and industrial operations, giving businesses access to transport infrastructure that could encourage further investment. Its opening marked an important step in turning the wider Alliance project into a functioning commercial development.A breakthrough came earlier that year, when American Airlines chairman Robert Crandall announced plans for a major aircraft maintenance facility at the airport. The investment was initially expected to create 4,500 jobs. Hillwood explained that the announcement helped establish confidence in Perot's plans. Although American Airlines eventually closed its maintenance centre in 2012, the wider Alliance development continued to expand, attracting businesses and generating employment across the region.Railways, warehouses and major companies fuelled AllianceTexas's growthAlliance's growth accelerated as additional transport infrastructure and commercial facilities arrived. In 1994, BNSF Railway opened an intermodal hub a few miles from the airport, strengthening the area's role in freight transport. FedEx also broke ground that year on a $300 million sorting hub at the airport, which was expected to employ at least 600 workers.These investments helped establish Alliance as a logistics centre, connecting air freight, rail transport and major road networks. The availability of industrial space and warehouses subsequently attracted more businesses, encouraging Hillwood to expand into residential and retail development as the area's workforce grew.According to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, at least 575 companies operated within Alliance, including Amazon, Walmart and LG Electronics. More than 14,600 homes had also been built within the development since 1990. The combination of employers, transport links and housing helped change northern Fort Worth from a largely rural landscape into a substantial business and residential corridor.How AllianceTexas generated billions in economic impact for North TexasBy December 2024, Alliance had grown far beyond the airport-centred project Perot first envisioned. Hillwood estimated that the development had generated $119.8 billion in economic impact for North Texas since its inception. The company also reported that the wider project had created more than 66,000 direct jobs over its history. The financial impact extended to local government. According to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, Alliance had generated more than $3.8 billion in property taxes across the region over three decades, including more than $752 million for the City of Fort Worth.The development had also attracted investment in retail and community facilities, including a shopping centre featuring Tarrant County's first H-E-B supermarket. Hillwood's business had expanded to include multi-family housing, property management and other services supporting the growing population. Despite the scale of the project, approximately one-third of Alliance remained undeveloped at the time of the 2024 report. Perot said he wished he had bought more land when he began the project, reflecting how dramatically the region had grown beyond its original rural setting.Alliance's future also remains a focus for Perot. In an interview with Fort Worth Business Journal in October 2026, the Hillwood chairman said he believed Fort Worth had significant room for further growth. He predicted that businesses the region had yet to imagine would eventually establish a presence there, describing the coming decades as particularly promising. His comments suggest that, despite Alliance's scale today, Perot continues to see substantial opportunities for expansion across Fort Worth and the surrounding region.How Ross Perot Jr.'s land investment helped reshape Fort WorthRoss Perot Jr.'s decision to buy land north of Fort Worth in 1985 laid the foundations for AllianceTexas, a development that grew through decades of investment in aviation, freight transport, industry, housing and retail. What had once been largely rural land became a major business centre with hundreds of companies and thousands of homes.The transformation was not immediate. It depended on attracting employers, building transport infrastructure and expanding the development as demand increased. By December 2024, Hillwood estimated that Alliance had generated $119.8 billion in economic impact for North Texas, illustrating the scale the project had reached.The story also highlights the importance of distinguishing AllianceTexas from other properties in Perot's portfolio. Although Circle T Ranch lies within the wider North Texas development landscape, the two approved sources do not establish the specific claim that Perot bought a 2,500-acre Circle T Ranch in 1993 for about $20 million. The documented history of Alliance itself provides a clear account of how his earlier land purchases helped reshape the region.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Libra Horoscope Today, October 18, 2026: Heavy workloads, new friendships and travel caution shape your day
articles.summary: General: You'll have to earn your peace today. The pace is busy, the mind is restless, and hard work may leave you more tense than satisfied by midday.
articles.body: General:You'll have to earn your peace today. The pace is busy, the mind is restless, and hard work may leave you more tense than satisfied by midday. The Moon is stirring your nerves, while Saturn brings pressure through tasks, calls, errands, and small obligations that keep piling up.Still, the day isn't without its sweet spots. New friendship is possible, and relations with neighbours can improve. There may be some celebration nearby, perhaps at a neighbour's house or in your lane or building, and you could end up being part of it. Life has its odd timing, doesn't it?Love and Relationship:Your mood can affect your relationships more than usual today. If you're rushed, hungry, or mentally scattered, you may speak sharply without meaning to. So pause before reacting. Venus doesn't deny warmth, but it asks you to choose it consciously.A new friend may enter the picture, or an old friend may reappear and lighten the day. If committed, don't dump all your stress on your partner in one conversation. Share, yes, but don't make them the punching bag for a difficult schedule. A calmer evening improves everything.Education and Career:This is a work-heavy day. Expect follow-ups, commuting strain, pending tasks, and maybe a few interruptions that break your flow. Keep a written list. If you try to hold everything in your head, tension will climb faster.Students may also feel restless. Study in short, disciplined blocks and avoid too many breaks. If you have group study, keep it serious. Otherwise it will become tea, gossip, and wasted time. Office workers should check messages before leaving any meeting. Details matter today.Money and Finance:This isn't a bad money day, but it is an unplanned-expense day if you're careless. Celebration spending, gifts, snacks, transport, and little convenience purchases can slip through your fingers like dry sand. Track them.Avoid buying food from outside just because you're too busy to think. Pack something from home if possible. It saves money and helps health, which needs protection now.Health and Well-being:Drive carefully. The warning is plain, and you should take it seriously. Restlessness plus traffic is a poor combination, especially if you're rushing between work and social calls. Leave a little early and don't check your phone while crossing roads or parking.Also, avoid outside food. Your digestion may not appreciate street snacks or oily meals today. Tension can already upset the system. Keep meals simple, drink water, and step away from noise whenever you can.Tip for the Day: Slow your pace on the road and lighten your dinner tonight.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. articles.title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as over 1,000 arrested after protests
articles.summary: Disorder broke out in cities across the country on a day in which more than half a million joined cost of living protests.
articles.body:
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against education standards and the cost of living.

At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.

In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.

Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.

Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeted against city halls and businesses also reported.

Sixty law enforcement officers were injured, including two who were taken to hospital unconscious, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.

In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".

However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.

Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.

Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.

In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".

Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.

Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.

A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."

The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.

Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.

Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.

Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.

Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.

On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups.

These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.

While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.

French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.

The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.

Watch: 'The mood has really shifted' at the Paris student protests

France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".

He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."

Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.

French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."

The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October.

However, the protests have continued and intensified.

articles.title: France protests turn violent: Fires, looting and 1,200 arrests; Macron vows action
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has vowed strict action against those involved in arson, looting and attacks on public buildings after violent clashes
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron has vowed strict action against those involved in arson, looting and attacks on public buildings after violent clashes erupted across France during nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services. More than 1,200 people were arrested as police clashed with protesters in Paris and several other cities on Saturday, with dozens of shops and public buildings damaged.The unrest, which also drew support from students protesting against school conditions and alleged excessive police force, saw officers deploy tear gas and water cannon to disperse masked demonstrators. Cars were set alight, businesses were ransacked and fires broke out in public buildings, including a town hall in Limoges, where part of the roof collapsed. France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez said 60 law enforcement officers were injured, including two who were taken to hospital unconscious.In a post on X on Sunday, Macron condemned the violence and backed security forces, saying those responsible for attacking public institutions and businesses would face prosecution and punishment. The unrest comes amid growing political uncertainty ahead of the next presidential election, with protesters accusing the government of failing to address economic pressures and public grievances.Macron, Lecornu warn rioters of consequences"No room for violence in our Republic," Macron wrote on X, adding that those who had attacked government offices, businesses and town halls would be "prosecuted and punished".He also expressed support for law enforcement personnel, describing them as guarantors of the right to demonstrate peacefully. Macron said the country would stand united against what he called "sowers of chaos", accusing them of seeking to undermine institutions and prevent peaceful protesters from voicing their demands.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also condemned the violence, blaming what he described as "ultraleft groups" and opportunistic rioters for orchestrating disturbances in several cities."Today, ultraleft groups have orchestrated violence in several French cities; delinquents have joined in to pillage and destroy," Lecornu wrote on X.He said police officers and gendarmes had faced violence of extreme intensity while protecting the public, adding that the government would not allow anyone to impose a political agenda through violence. Lecornu also backed the proposed "pay-the-damagers" bill, which seeks to make those responsible for destruction bear the financial cost of the damage."Public money is scarce: it must fund our public services, not endlessly repair what vandals destroy. It is up to them to bear the cost," he said.Clashes spread across French citiesAccording to France 24, violence broke out in several cities after hundreds of thousands of people joined the demonstrations. The CGT trade union estimated that around 550,000 people took part nationwide, although authorities had not immediately released their own estimate.In Paris, riot police used tear gas and water cannon against groups throwing fireworks and other projectiles. A bar was set on fire, parked vehicles were torched and looting was reported at several businesses. An Apple store in Lille was among the shops targeted, while a tourist office in Lyon was set ablaze. Town halls in Marseille and Lille were also vandalised.In Saint-Etienne, a male demonstrator reportedly lost a hand after a police crowd-control grenade exploded, according to a police source cited by AFP. The incident followed a similar injury to a 15-year-old during an earlier protest in Lens.Despite the violence, many demonstrators marched peacefully, calling for higher wages, lower prices and better public services. Some protesters said they were frustrated by the government's failure to address their concerns.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
